title: Data Center Is Fined $1.1 Million for Operating 62 Power Generators

reading.body:
This is a permitting and compliance failure at the physical infrastructure layer of a data center deployment, not a failure of a model or of software. Sixty-two natural gas generators, each rated at 2,000 kilowatts and roughly the size of a tractor trailer, were installed and operated at the Vineland site without permits to be installed or operated. State inspectors found them in late July, and New Jersey issued a $1.07 million penalty under the Air Pollution Control Act, which officials described as the largest ever issued to a data center operator in the state. The campus is partly in use and is planned to reach 2.6 million square feet and 350 megawatts.

Catching this would have required confirming that installation and operating permits existed before the generators were run, and an inspection that reached the site earlier in the build. The equipment is large, fixed and individually countable, so the failure was one of authorisation and oversight rather than of detection difficulty.

What is not established is intent. The homeowners' federal lawsuit over noise is an allegation and not a finding, and the Cumberland County Health Department's noise violation orders are a separate matter from the air permit penalty. The reporting does not establish how long the generators had been operating or what computing workload the site serves.

reports.title: Data Center Is Fined $1.1 Million for Operating 62 Power Generators

summary:
New Jersey fined DataOne $1.07 million after state inspectors found 62 natural gas generators at its Vineland data center site in late July. The 2,000 kilowatt generators, each about the size of a tractor trailer, lacked permits to be installed or operated. Officials said the penalty for violating the Air Pollution Control Act is the largest ever issued to a data center operator in New Jersey.

The planned 2.6 million square foot campus is set to be completed at the end of the year and will need 350 megawatts, enough to power a medium size city. Some of it is already in use. Homeowners have filed a federal lawsuit over persistent noise, and the Cumberland County Health Department issued violation orders for excessive noise. Governor Mikie Sherrill said data center growth must benefit New Jersey communities.
